description: Known answers for geo.distance and geo.in_zone (ADR-P4-9), read by core/tests/test_geo.c (through core/tests/geo_vectors.h, made by tools/protogen.py) and simulator/tests/test_geo.py. 'metres' and 'inside' come from the cited source, never from the implementation; a distance passes within tolerance_m. 'bits' is the IEEE 754 double the implementation returns, the same on every platform (decision M3-1): a determinism pin, checked exactly, not a known answer.

distances.name: bna_lax
distances.source: Rosetta Code, 'Haversine formula' task (https://rosettacode.org/wiki/Haversine_formula): BNA (36.12, -86.67) to LAX (33.94, -118.40), '6371.0 km -> 2886.44444283798329974715782394574671655 km'

distances.name: jfk_sin_wgs84
distances.source: GeographicLib GeodSolve(1) manual, EXAMPLES (https://geographiclib.sourceforge.io/C++/doc/GeodSolve.1.html): JFK 40:38:23N 073:46:44W to SIN 01:21:33N 103:59:22E is 15347628 m on the WGS84 ellipsoid; the sphere is within ADR-P4-9's 0.5 %

distances.name: meridian_1m
distances.source: Along a meridian the haversine distance is R * dlat (dlat in radians), so lat + 1 m * 180 / (pi * 6371000 m) is 1 m away

distances.name: meridian_100m
distances.source: As meridian_1m, 100 m

distances.name: equator_100m
distances.source: Along the equator the haversine distance is R * dlon, so 100 m * 180 / (pi * 6371000 m) of longitude is 100 m

distances.name: same_point
distances.source: A point is 0 m from itself

distances.name: antipodes_equator
distances.source: Antipodes are half a great circle apart: pi * 6371000 m = 20015086.796... m

distances.name: antipodes_poles
distances.source: As antipodes_equator, pole to pole

distances.name: antipodes_lisbon
distances.source: As antipodes_equator; haversine is ill-conditioned next to antipodes, hence 1 m

distances.name: across_180
distances.source: 0.2 degrees of longitude across the 180th meridian at 10 N: about R * cos(10 deg) * 0.2 deg (a parallel's arc, longer than the great circle by under 1 mm)
